articles.label: Government
articles.headline: Escambia County's $47 million in federal grants hangs in limbo as Washington stalls
articles.dek: Local infrastructure projects approved under the bipartisan bill face uncertain futures. County administrators are making contingency plans.
brief: Seven Escambia County projects totaling $47.3 million in approved federal grants now face funding freezes or cancellation
County Administrator Wes Moreno confirms contingency planning underway, including potential property tax increases
The Beulah sewer extension and Cervantes Street corridor improvements are among projects most at risk
articles.body:
The paperwork sits in a filing cabinet on the third floor of the Escambia County Administrative Complex. Seven project folders. Signed agreements. Federal grant awards totaling $47.3 million. All of it approved, allocated and ready to move.

None of it is coming.

Since February, the Office of Management and Budget has frozen disbursements on Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act grants pending what the administration calls a "comprehensive review of federal spending priorities." For Escambia County, that bureaucratic language translates to something simpler: projects that were supposed to break ground this year now exist only on paper.

"We did everything right," County Administrator Wes Moreno said Tuesday. "We applied. We competed. We won these grants. And now we're being told to wait indefinitely."

What's at stake

The largest single award—$18.7 million for the Beulah sewer extension—would have brought municipal wastewater service to 4,200 households currently relying on septic systems. Engineers completed the design work last fall. Easement negotiations with property owners wrapped up in January. The county had already issued the bid package when the freeze hit.

"We were three weeks from selecting a contractor," said Amy Patterson, director of the county's engineering division. "Three weeks."

The other frozen projects include:

  • $12.4 million for Cervantes Street corridor improvements between Pace Boulevard and A Street
  • $6.8 million for stormwater drainage upgrades in the Warrington area
  • $4.1 million for bridge repairs on Muscogee Road
  • $3.2 million for pedestrian safety improvements near Workman Middle School
  • $1.4 million for ADA accessibility upgrades at county facilities
  • $700,000 for electric vehicle charging stations at public parks

The Cervantes project had already seen preliminary work. Surveyors staked the right-of-way. Utility relocations were scheduled. Now orange flags fade in the sun along an unchanged roadway.

The federal picture

Escambia County is not alone. Across Florida, 143 local governments are waiting on $2.1 billion in frozen IIJA funds, according to data compiled by the Florida Association of Counties. Nationally, the figure exceeds $38 billion.

The OMB has not provided a timeline for completing its review. Requests for comment from the agency went unanswered. Congressional representatives have offered little clarity.

U.S. Rep. Matt Gaetz, whose district includes Escambia County, released a statement in March supporting "fiscal responsibility in infrastructure spending" but did not address specific local projects. His office did not respond to follow-up inquiries.

Sen. Rick Scott's office confirmed the senator had "raised concerns" with OMB Director Russell Vought but provided no details on those conversations.

Local contingencies

Behind closed doors, county staff have begun planning for a future where the federal money never arrives.

A draft memo obtained by The Flightline outlines three scenarios. The first assumes full funding arrives by October—county administrators privately assign this outcome a probability of less than 20 percent. The second envisions partial funding with extended timelines. The third prepares for total loss of the grants.

Under the worst-case scenario, the county would face difficult choices. The Beulah sewer project alone would require either a 0.4-mill property tax increase sustained over 15 years or the creation of a special taxing district for affected residents. Either option would require commission approval and, in the case of the taxing district, a referendum.

"Nobody wants to talk about raising taxes," Moreno said. "But these projects address real problems. Septic failures. Flooding. Bridges that won't pass inspection forever. The needs don't go away because Washington can't get its act together."

Commissioner Jeff Bergosh, whose district includes Beulah, said he's fielding calls from frustrated constituents weekly.

"These folks were told relief was coming," Bergosh said. "Some of them have been dealing with failing septic systems for years. They did the right thing. They waited for the government solution instead of paying $30,000 out of pocket. And now what do I tell them?"

Contracts and consequences

The freeze carries costs beyond the obvious. Engineering firms completed design work under contracts that assumed construction would follow. Those firms billed the county $1.2 million for services rendered. The county paid.

If the projects never move forward, that money buys nothing but drawings that will eventually require updating.

"Design documents have a shelf life," Patterson said. "Codes change. Conditions change. If we're sitting here in 2028 and funding finally comes through, we might be starting the engineering from scratch."

Contractors who anticipated bidding on county work have adjusted their own plans. Marcus Williams, president of Gulf South Construction, said his company hired 14 workers last fall in anticipation of the Cervantes project.

"We based that on public information," Williams said. "The county announced these projects. They put out bid packages. We staffed up to compete. Now those guys are working other jobs or they're gone."

Williams said his company will be more cautious about federal projects going forward. "You can't run a business on promises from Washington."

What happens next

The county commission will receive a formal briefing on the grant situation at its July 15 meeting. Staff will present the contingency scenarios and request direction.

Commissioner Steven Barry said he wants to see the full picture before committing to any path forward.

"We're not going to panic," Barry said. "But we're also not going to pretend everything's fine. The residents of this county deserve honest answers about what we can and can't deliver."

For now, the project folders remain in their cabinet. The orange survey flags along Cervantes Street continue their slow fade. And 4,200 households in Beulah wait for a sewer system that may or may not arrive.

The federal government made a promise. Whether it keeps that promise is no longer a question Escambia County can answer.

articles.label: Pensacola Beach
articles.headline: Fourth of July returns to Pensacola Beach after two years of permit fights
articles.dek: The fireworks are back, but the battle over who controls the island's biggest night isn't over.
brief: Pensacola Beach will host its first official Fourth of July fireworks since 2023 after a two-year hiatus caused by disputes between Santa Rosa Island Authority and Escambia County over event permits and liability.
The compromise reached in May grants SRIA primary control over beach events but requires county approval for fireworks displays exceeding $50,000 in cost.
Local businesses estimate the two-year gap cost the beach economy between $3 million and $5 million in lost holiday weekend revenue.
articles.body:
The barge sits a half-mile off Casino Beach, loaded with 4,000 shells waiting for tomorrow night. Workers in orange vests finished securing the mortars Wednesday afternoon while tourists on paddleboards drifted close enough to get waved off by a Coast Guard auxiliary boat.

It's been two years since fireworks lit up Pensacola Beach on the Fourth of July. Two years of empty bleachers and dark skies and locals driving to Navarre or Orange Beach to watch someone else's show. Two years of meetings, lawyers, and finger-pointing between the Santa Rosa Island Authority and Escambia County over a question that should have been simple: Who gets to throw the party?

"We're just glad it's happening," said Maria Santos, general manager of Flounder's Chowder House. She stood on the restaurant's deck Thursday morning, watching her staff set up extra tables for what she expects will be their busiest weekend since 2023. "But I'd be lying if I said we weren't nervous. Everyone's nervous."

The split

The fight started over insurance.

In March 2024, Escambia County informed SRIA that it would no longer extend its liability coverage to events the authority organized on the beach. The county cited rising premiums and a 2023 incident during the Blue Angels air show when a spectator fell from a temporary structure and filed suit.

SRIA, the quasi-governmental body that manages Pensacola Beach's leaseholds, had operated the Fourth of July celebration for 31 consecutive years. Fireworks. Live music on the main stage. The whole production ran through their office, with county support on traffic control and emergency services.

Without county insurance, SRIA faced the choice of purchasing its own $2 million event policy or canceling. They canceled.

"We were given six weeks' notice," said SRIA Executive Director Paolo Ghio. "That's not enough time to procure independent coverage for an event of that scale. We had no choice."

County officials disputed the timeline. Then-County Administrator Wes Moreno told commissioners in April 2024 that SRIA had been warned "multiple times" about the insurance changes as early as January.

The back-and-forth continued through 2025. SRIA organized a smaller Memorial Day concert that year, paying $47,000 for its own policy. But negotiations over Fourth of July collapsed again in May 2025 when the two sides couldn't agree on cost-sharing for sheriff's deputies and fire rescue staging.

"It became about control," said one SRIA board member who requested anonymity to discuss internal deliberations. "The county wanted veto power over our events. We weren't willing to give that up."

The compromise

The breakthrough came in February. New Escambia County Administrator Diane Hutchinson, who took over after Moreno's retirement, proposed a tiered system. Events under $50,000 would remain under SRIA's sole authority. Anything larger would require a joint approval process—but SRIA would retain operational control.

The county commission approved the framework 4-1 in March. Commissioner Jeff Bergosh cast the only no vote, calling it "a half-measure that kicks the can down the road."

SRIA moved quickly. By late March, they had contracted with Pyro Spectaculars, the same company that handled the show through 2023. The county agreed to cover 40 percent of the $180,000 production cost—less than its pre-2024 contribution of 50 percent, but enough to close the deal.

"It's not perfect," Ghio acknowledged. "But we're back in business."

What was lost

The two-year gap left marks.

Santos estimates Flounder's lost $400,000 in revenue across both canceled holidays. Bamboo Willie's, the beachfront bar at the Boardwalk, saw similar declines. Owner Mark Williams said Fourth of July weekend typically accounted for 8 percent of his annual gross.

"You can't make that up," Williams said. "Christmas doesn't bring those numbers. Spring break doesn't bring those numbers. Fourth of July does."

The Pensacola Beach Chamber of Commerce commissioned a study last fall estimating total economic losses across both years at $3.2 million to $4.8 million. The methodology relied on hotel booking data, restaurant receipts, and parking revenues from previous years.

Some businesses didn't survive to see the fireworks return. Sandy's Beach Shack, a souvenir shop that had operated near the fishing pier since 1998, closed permanently in October 2025. Owner Sandra Keller cited the consecutive bad summers as the final blow.

"We were hanging on by our fingernails after COVID," Keller told The Flightline in a phone interview from her new home in Tallahassee. "Two more bad Julys finished us."

Tomorrow night

The show starts at 9 p.m. Pyro Spectaculars promises 22 minutes of continuous display, the longest in the event's history. The main stage will feature three local bands starting at 5 p.m. Food trucks line Via de Luna from the traffic circle to Avenida 10.

SRIA expects 35,000 to 40,000 people on the beach. The sheriff's office will have 28 deputies on overtime. Escambia County EMS is staging three additional ambulances at the public safety building on Fort Pickens Road.

The forecast calls for partly cloudy skies, high of 91, 20 percent chance of afternoon thunderstorms clearing by evening. Standard summer fare.

At the Pensacola Beach Gulf Pier, manager Tom Rodriguez was hosing down the deck Thursday afternoon, prepping for crowds that would start arriving before dawn Friday. He's worked the pier for 14 Fourth of Julys. The two quiet ones felt wrong.

"People come here expecting something," Rodriguez said. "They expect the fireworks, the music, the whole thing. When it's not there, they feel cheated. Even if it's not your fault. Even if you explain why. They still feel cheated."

He turned off the hose and looked out at the barge.

"Tomorrow, nobody feels cheated."

What comes next

The détente between SRIA and Escambia County holds for now. Both sides describe the relationship as "professional" rather than warm. The joint approval process has already been invoked twice since March—once for tomorrow's fireworks, once for a Labor Day concert still in planning stages.

But the underlying tension hasn't resolved. SRIA still wants full autonomy over beach events. The county still wants oversight of anything that draws large crowds and requires emergency services. Neither side has moved off those positions.

Commissioner Bergosh has called for a full review of SRIA's governance structure, suggesting the authority should be folded into county government entirely. The proposal has little support on the current commission but remains in the public discussion.

"We'll deal with that later," Ghio said. "Right now, we've got a show to put on."

Out on Casino Beach, the bleachers went up Thursday afternoon. Volunteers from Pensacola Beach Advocates planted small American flags along the dune line. A crew from Gulf Power tested the temporary lighting rigs that would illuminate the stage.

The barge sat steady in the Gulf, ready.

articles.label: Investigation
articles.headline: Downtown Pensacola's empty storefronts: Who owns them and why they stay dark
articles.dek: A Flightline review of property records reveals a pattern of out-of-state investors holding prime Palafox real estate while local businesses scramble for space.
brief: Seventeen storefronts along Palafox Street between Garden and Main have sat vacant for more than 18 months, according to Flightline analysis of city business license records.
Property records show 12 of those 17 spaces are owned by LLCs registered outside Florida, with the largest concentration tied to holding companies in Delaware and Texas.
Local business owners report being quoted rents of $35 to $45 per square foot for spaces that sat empty throughout 2025, pricing that exceeds comparable retail corridors in Mobile and Tallahassee.
articles.body:
The storefront at 220 South Palafox has been dark for 31 months. Brown paper covers the windows. A faded "For Lease" sign lists a Houston area code.

Three doors down, another empty space. Across the street, two more. Walk the six blocks of Palafox between Garden Street and Main Street on any given Tuesday afternoon and you'll count at least a dozen businesses that aren't there.

A Flightline review of Escambia County property records, Florida Division of Corporations filings and City of Pensacola business license data reveals a pattern behind these dark windows: out-of-state investment groups purchasing prime downtown real estate, then holding it vacant at asking rents local operators say they cannot afford.

Following the paper trail

The Flightline identified 17 ground-floor commercial spaces along the Palafox corridor that have been continuously vacant since at least January 2025. Of those 17, property records show 12 are owned by limited liability companies registered outside Florida.

The largest single holder is Meridian Gulf Properties LLC, a Delaware corporation that acquired four adjacent storefronts near the Saenger Theatre in 2023. State records list a registered agent in Wilmington. The company has no listed Florida phone number or local representative.

Attempts to reach Meridian Gulf Properties through its registered agent went unanswered over a three-week period.

Three additional properties are held by 311 Palafox Holdings LP, a Texas limited partnership with a mailing address in a Houston office tower. Two more belong to a Nevada LLC called Emerald Coast Retail Partners, despite having no apparent connection to the Emerald Coast region beyond these purchases.

None of these entities responded to written requests for comment.

'They'd rather sit empty'

Maria Sandoval spent eight months trying to lease a 1,400-square-foot space for a specialty grocery concept. She said she was quoted $42 per square foot annually for a storefront on South Palafox that had been vacant since 2024.

"I ran the numbers six different ways," Sandoval said. "There's no version where that works for a small grocery. They'd rather sit empty than negotiate."

Sandoval eventually signed a lease in East Hill. The Palafox space remains unoccupied.

Commercial real estate broker Tom Kendrick, who represents tenants seeking downtown space, confirmed what he called "a holding pattern" among some out-of-state owners.

"They bought at what they considered a discount during COVID, and they're carrying these properties with cheap money," Kendrick said. "Their basis is so low they don't feel pressure to fill the space at market-clearing rents."

Kendrick said asking rents on Palafox have increased roughly 40% since 2019, while vacancy rates have remained stubbornly high. He attributed the disconnect to owners who are "investing in an idea of Pensacola, not operating in the reality of Pensacola."

Comparable markets

The Flightline reviewed commercial lease listings in downtown Mobile, Alabama and the College Town district of Tallahassee—two markets with similar population bases and tourism profiles.

In Mobile's Dauphin Street corridor, asking rents for comparable ground-floor retail averaged $24 to $28 per square foot in current listings. In Tallahassee's College Town, rates ran $26 to $32 per square foot.

The Palafox spaces reviewed by The Flightline were listed between $35 and $48 per square foot.

Scott Petrillo operates a bicycle shop two blocks off Palafox. He said he looked at moving to the main corridor in 2025 but couldn't make the economics work.

"I'd be paying twice what I pay now for maybe 20% more foot traffic," Petrillo said. "And half those people are tourists who aren't buying a $2,000 bike anyway."

City Hall's limited toolkit

Pensacola City Council member Jennifer Brahney represents District 6, which includes most of downtown. She said she has fielded complaints about the vacancy problem for years but acknowledged the city has few tools to compel owners to fill empty spaces.

"We can't force someone to lease their property at a price we think is fair," Brahney said. "That's not how property rights work in Florida."

The city does impose higher property tax assessments on commercial properties that are not occupied by an active business, but the differential is modest. Brahney said she has discussed more aggressive vacancy fees with city staff but described the legal and political path as "complicated."

"You start talking about penalizing property owners and you get a lot of pushback," she said.

City economic development director Marcus Webb said his office focuses on recruiting businesses that can afford existing rents rather than attempting to influence property owners.

"Our job is to make downtown attractive to investment," Webb said in an email. "We're not in the business of regulating what someone charges for their own property."

A waiting game

Kendrick, the commercial broker, said some out-of-state owners appear to be holding properties in anticipation of eventual sale rather than rental income. Downtown Pensacola land values have appreciated steadily since 2020, even as retail occupancy has stagnated.

"You can make a return just on the appreciation," Kendrick said. "The rent is almost a nuisance at that point. Why deal with a tenant who might miss payments when you can just wait for the next buyer?"

Property records show several downtown parcels have changed hands between out-of-state entities without ever hosting an operating business during the holding period.

The storefront at 220 South Palafox, the one with the Houston phone number on the sign, sold in 2024 for $1.2 million. The buyer was a Delaware LLC called Southern Palms Capital. The seller was another Delaware LLC called Bayshore Main Street Partners.

Neither entity has filed for a business license in Pensacola. The space remains empty.

What locals see

On a Thursday evening in late June, Palafox Street showed its split personality. The blocks near Seville Quarter hummed with restaurant crowds and live music. But the stretch between Intendencia and Main was quieter, foot traffic thinning past darkened windows.

Robert Chen was walking his dog past a vacant storefront that used to be a bookstore. He's lived downtown for six years.

"It's frustrating," Chen said. "You see all these articles about downtown's revitalization, and then you walk past four empty stores to get your coffee."

He paused, looking at the brown paper covering the windows.

"Someone's making money here," he said. "I just don't think it's anyone who actually lives in Pensacola."
